analytic.title: Preemptive uniprocessor scheduling of non-cyclic GMF task systems *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Formal models used for representing recurrent real-time processes are typically characterized by a period parameter, representing the minimum amount of time that may elapse between successive invocations of the process. However a recently proposed model called the non-cyclic GMF model deviates from this trend: there is no single period parameter characterizing the recurrent behavior of the task. In this paper we consider schedulability analysis of real-time systems comprised of collections of such tasks, that are to be scheduled using earliest-deadline first (EDF) scheduling on a single preemptive processor. We provide evidence that indicates that schedulability analysis for such systems is more difficult than for systems in which each recurrent task is characterized by a single period parameter, and derive a pseudo-polynomial time schedulability analysis algorithm for bounded-utilization systems of such tasks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many real-time systems can be modeled as being comprised of a finite number of independent recurrent processes or tasks, each of which generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs. Different formal models have been proposed for representing such recurrent tasks; these models differ from one another in the restrictions they place on the jobs that may be generated by a single task. Models that have previously been proposed include the implicitdeadline model [10] (also sometimes called the Liu and Layland model), the sporadic tasks model [11], the multiframe model [12], and the generalized multiframe (GMF) model [4]. Since the model studied in this paper is a modification to the GMF model, we now describe the GMF model (details concerning the other models are available in the primary sources cited above.)

In the GMF model, a recurrent task τ i is characterized by the 3-tuple ( C i , D i , T i ), where C i , D i and T i are N i -ary vectors of positive real numbers: [C i (0), C i (1), . . . , C i (N i -1)] represent execution requirements, [D i (0), D i (1), . . . , D i (N i -1)] represent (relative) deadlines, and [T i (0), T i (1), . . . , T i (N i -1)] represent minimum separations between successive job arrivals. The interpretation is as follows: The j'th job generated by task τ i has a release time a j , a deadline a j + d j , and a worst-case execution time (WCET) requirement of c j , where
• a 0 ≥ 0, and a j+1 ≥ a j + T i (j mod N i ),
• d j = D i (j mod N i ), and
div.formula: • c j = C i (j mod N i ).
div.p: Informally, such a task's parameters can be thought of as specifying N i different kinds of jobs; the task generates an infinite sequence of jobs by cycling through these different kinds of jobs in the specified order. It has been shown in [4] that the GMF model is a strict generalization of the earlier Liu and Layland, sporadic tasks, and multiframe models.

Although the GMF model allows a single recurrent task to generate different kinds of jobs, it restricts the order in which these jobs may be generated: given the parameters of the job last released by a GMF task, the WCET and relative deadline (i.e., the length of the duration between its release time and its deadline) of the next job released by this task is fixed although its release time is only bounded from below. Assuming that each such (WCET, relative deadline pair) corresponds to a different piece of code, this implies that although the time at which these pieces of code are executed is determined by run-time events, the order in which they will execute is pre-determined during system design time.

In the context of some work concerning the modeling of the processes that comprise a software-defined radio (SDR), Moyo et al. [13,14] discovered that this restriction is overly restrictive -not only the release time, but also the identity of the next job to be generated by a task should be allowed to be determined by run-time events. They proposed a new model that they call non-cyclic GMF [13,14]. A task τ i in this model is characterized by three equi-sized vectors ( C i , D i , T i ) exactly as in the GMF model; however, the interpretation of these vectors is somewhat differ-ent. Informally, each task generates an infinite sequence of jobs, whose parameters are as specified in the three vectors. However, unlike in the GMF model there is no predetermined order in which parameters of these generated jobs are selected from the corresponding vectors. That is, as in the (regular) GMF model there are N i different kinds of jobs that can be generated by τ i : the k'th kind has a WCET equal to C i (k) and a deadline that occurs D i (k) time units after its arrival-instant; furthermore, this job constrains that the next job generated by τ i will not be released until at least T i (k) time units have elapsed since its own release. However, the next job may be of any one of the N i kinds of jobs (including the same kind as the current job).

Moyo et al. [13,14] make a persuasive case that the non-cyclic GMF model better models the behavior of some event-driven systems, such as SDR, in which the characteristics of the next job generated is likely to depend on external triggering events during run-time and cannot always be predicted during system design time. Modeling such systems using the GMF model to represent such an application, it can be shown, is pessimistic in the sense that it results in suboptimal use of platform computing capabilities.

Task models (typically based on directed acyclic graphs or DAG's) have previously been proposed for representing real-time code containing branches, in which the precise execution path taken depends during any particular execution on the occurrence of run-time events. However, as far as we are aware all such models assume that the entire task is characterized by a single "period" parameter indicating the minimum amount of time that must elapse between successive invocations of the task; to our knowledge, the non-cyclic GMF model is the first model for recurrent tasks considered by the real-time scheduling community, in which each recurrent task is not characterized by a single period parameter (thereby ruling out the possibility of modeling its behavior by a cyclic schedule) 1 . Moyo et al. [13,14] call their model non-cyclic to highlight this lack of any obvious periodicity to the task's behavior. This fact -that system behavior need not be cyclic -is also why this model is not simply a special case of these prior DAG-based models for conditional real-time tasks. This research. In this paper, we consider the scheduling, upon a single preemptive processor, of real-time systems that can be modeled as collections of independent noncyclic GMF tasks. We show the relationship of the noncyclic GMF task model to other models that have previously been proposed for representing recurrent real-time code, and provide evidence indicating that analysis for the noncyclic GMF task models is inherently more difficult than for all these other models. We design an exact EDF schedulability test that runs in pseudo-polynomial time for systems of non-cyclic GMF tasks satisfying the additional property that the asymptotic processor utilization of the task system is bounded from above by a constant strictly less than computational capacity of the processor.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we describe the non-cyclic GMF model, and define some additional terminology and notation that we will be using throughout the remainder of this paper. In Section 3 we explain how the non-cyclic GMF model fits in with other models that have previously been proposed for representing recurrent real-time processes, and highlight why we believe that this model is a particularly significant one. In Section 4 we consider the problem of computing the demand bound function, which quantifies the computational demand of a real-time task over any interval of a given length as a function of the interval-length, for non-cyclic GMF tasks. We prove that in contrast to previously-studied models, determining the demand bound function of a noncyclic GMF task is computationally intractable (NP hard). In Section 5 we derive an EDF schedulability analysis algorithm for systems of non-cyclic GMF tasks implemented on a single preemptive processor, and characterize the run-time complexity of this algorithm.

div.head: The non-cyclic GMF task model
div.p: As stated in Section 1 above, a non-cyclic GMF task τ i is characterized by three equi-sized vectors ( C i , D i , T i ), each of size N i . In this paper, we assume for ease of exposition that these are vectors of positive integers, although our results hold even if these parameters are rationals rather than integers. Such a task τ i generates an infinite sequence of jobs. Let ν : N → {0, 1, . . . , N i -1} denote any infinite sequence of the numbers {0, 1, . . . , N i -1}. Task τ i can legally generate a sequence of jobs corresponding to this sequence ν. The j'th job of task τ i in such a sequence of jobs has a release time a j , a deadline a j + d j , and a WCET of c j , satisfying the properties that • a 0 ≥ 0, and a j+1 ≥ a j + T i (ν(j)),
• d j = D i (ν(j)), and

The original GMF model [4] is a special case of this model, in the sense that in the original GMF model ν(j) = (j mod N i ) for all j ≥ 0. Since it was shown in [4] that the original GMF model generalizes the Liu and Layland, sporadic, and multiframe models, it immediately follows that the non-cyclic GMF model also generalizes all these prior models as well.

Example 1 Consider a non-cyclic GMF task τ i specified as follows: ([1, 2, 3], [4,2,6], [4,5,7]). For this task, [4,2,6], and T i = [4,5,7]. Such a task can generate 3 different kinds of jobs, requiring either (i) 1 unit of execution within the next 4 time units; (ii) 2 units of execution immediately upon its release; or (iii) 3 units of execution within the next 6 time units. The task releases an infinite sequence of jobs of these three kinds, in any order. At least 4, 5, and 7 time units must elapse respectively after the release of a job of the first, second, or third kind respectively, before the release of the next job by this task. We will refer to the time interval [a j , a j + D i (ν(j))) as the scheduling window, and the time interval [a j , a j + T i (ν(j))) as the exclusion window, of the j'th job in this arrival sequence. We highlight the fact that the non-cyclic GMF model does not mandate that the scheduling window of a job be contained within its exclusion window (equivalently, it is not required that D i (k) be ≤ T i (k) for all k). That is, in the terminology that is widely used with respect to sporadic tasks [11] we do not require constrained deadlines but allow for the more general arbitrary deadlines.

In this paper, we are concerned with preemptive uniprocessor EDF schedulability of systems of non-cyclic GMF tasks. That is, we are given a collection τ = {τ i = ( C i , D i , T i )} n i=1 of n non-cyclic GMF tasks and wish to determine whether the system is guaranteed to be scheduled by EDF on a preemptive processor such that all jobs of all tasks will always complete by their deadlines, for every instance of jobs that can legally be generated by these tasks 2 .

Since the non-cyclic GMF model is a generalization of the sporadic task model, it follows from the recent results of Eisenbrand and Rothvoß [7] that it is coNP-hard to determine preemptive uniprocessor EDF schedulability for systems of non-cyclic GMF tasks. Hence, we should not expect to be able to come up with polynomial-time exact (i.e., necessary and sufficient) schedulability tests. Some further definitions: let us define the utilization U i of non-cyclic GMF task τ i to be the largest ratio of the Liu & Layland [10] sporadic [11] multiframe [12] generalized multiframe (GMF) [4] non-cyclic GMF recurring real-time [ WCET to exclusion window size of any job that can be generated by it:
div.formula: U i = max (j : 0≤j<N i ) C i (j) T i (j) .
div.p: The utilization of the task τ i of Example 1 is max{1/4, 2/5, 3/7} = 3/7.
The utilization U (τ ) of task system τ is the sum of the utilizations of all the tasks in τ :
Let us define the largest WCET C max i of non-cyclic GMF task τ i to be the largest WCET of any job that can be generated by it:
div.formula: C max i = max (j : 0≤j<N i ) C i (j) . For the task τ i of Example 1, C max i = max{1, 2, 3} = 3.

div.head: Context and significance
div.p: Many formal models have been proposed over the years for representing recurrent real-time tasks that are to be implemented on preemptive uniprocessor platforms. These include the Liu & Layland model, the sporadic tasks model, the multiframe tasks model, the generalized multiframe tasks model and the recurring real-time tasks model [2,3].

While these models differ from one another in their expressive abilities -i.e., what features of actual systems each model is able to represent accurately -a common feature of all these models is that EDF schedulability analysis is tractable, where "tractable" is assumed to mean no worse than pseudo-polynomial time for bounded-utilization 3 sys-tems. In this context, the recurring real-time tasks model was considered the "most general" tractable model, in the sense that it generalizes earlier tractable models -see Figure 1.

(The anisochronous task model of Anand et al. [1] can also be considered as a generalization, in a different direction, of the GMF model. However, as pointed out in Section 1, [1] deals with this generalization by approximating the behavior of an anisochronous task by a task that is a special form of the recurring real-time task [3]. Thus while the anisochronous model is a generalization of the GMF model, the analysis of this model in [1] is a special case of the analysis for the recurring real-time model [3].)

The task model discussed in this paper -the non-cyclic GMF tasks model -generalizes the GMF task model in a different direction from the direction that the recurring realtime tasks model. The EDF schedulability analysis algorithms for systems of non-cyclic tasks that were presented in [13,14] have exponential-time complexity. However, we will show in this paper that EDF schedulability analysis for non-cyclic GMF task systems is also in pseudopolynomial time for bounded-utilization systems; accordingly, this model, too, is considered tractable. This factthat generalization to allow non-cyclicity retains the property of tractability of analysis -is interesting in and of itself; in addition, it leaves open the possibility of obtaining further generalizations along this direction while retaining tractability.

div.head: Demand Bound Function
div.p: The concept of the demand bound function, or DBF, has previously been used to quantify the maximum amount of computing capacity that could be required by jobs of a recurrent task over any contiguous time interval:

div.head: Definition 1 (Demand bound function (DBF)) For any recurrent task (including a non-cyclic GMF task) τ i and any positive integer t, DBF i (t) is a non-negative integer denoting the maximum cumulative execution requirement by jobs of τ that can arrive in, and have their deadlines within, any contiguous time interval of length at most t.
div.p: Example 2 We illustrate some DBF i (t) computations for the non-cyclic GMF task τ i of Example 1:
• DBF i (t) = 0 for all t < 2, since no job if τ i has a scheduling window of size < 2.
• DBF i (t) ≥ 2 for 2 ≤ t < 6 since a job of the second kind arriving at the start of the interval and would have its deadline within such an interval.
• DBF i (t) ≥ 3, for t = 6 since a job of the third kind arriving at the start of the interval and would have its deadline within an interval of size 6.

• DBF i (t) ≥ 4 for 7 ≤ t < 9 since a job of the second kind arriving at the start of the interval, followed by another arriving as soon as permitted to do so (i.e., 5 time units into the interval) would both have their deadlines within such an interval.

• DBF i (t) ≥ 5 for 9 ≤ t < 12 since a job of the third kind arriving at the start of the interval, followed by one of the second kind arriving as soon as permitted to do so (i.e., 7 time units into the interval) would both have their deadlines within such an interval.

• DBF i (t) ≥ 6 for t = 12 since a job of the second kind arriving at the start of the interval, followed by two others each arriving as soon as permitted to do so (i.e., 5 and 10 time units into the interval) would all have their deadlines within such an interval.

The DBF computations in Example 2 were done by inspection: all possible job-release sequences were considered, and the one maximizing the cumulative execution requirement within the interval was selected. Clearly, such exhaustive enumeration and trial and error are not effective procedures for computing DBF (indeed, although the job release sequences listed in the example above illustrate that the values for DBF i (t) listed above are clearly lower bounds on the actual values, these examples do not rule out the possibility that there may be other job release sequences that would result in a higher value of DBF i (t).) We would like an efficient, methodical approach to computing DBF i (t) for non-cyclic GMF task τ i and given t.

It is known that the demand bound function can be easily determined for recurrent tasks specified in the Liu and Layland, sporadic, multiframe (MF), and generalized multiframe (GMF) models. For instance, for a Liu and Layland task τ i = (C i , T i ) (the reader not familiar with this notation can see, e.g., [10] for an explanation), DBF i (t) = C i × t T i . A similar closed-form expression is known [5] for determining DBF i (t) for a sporadic task τ i . For MF and GMF tasks, a preprocessing algorithm that runs in polynomial time is described in [4]; once such preprocessing has been done, it is described how DBF i (t) can be determined in constant time for any t.

For non-cyclic GMF tasks, unfortunately, computing the demand bound function is more challenging. In fact, given an arbitrary non-cyclic GMF task τ i and an arbitrary positive integer t, DBF i (t) cannot be determined in polynomial time unless P = NP (a proof of this fact is provided in the appendix). In the remainder of this section, we derive an algorithm for computing demand bound function for noncyclic GMF tasks, that has pseudo-polynomial run-time.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: For any recurrent task system comprised of independent tasks in which minimum, rather than exact, durations are specified between the release times of consecutive jobs of the same task, a synchronous arrival sequence of jobs is defined as a collection of jobs generated by the task system in which 1. Each task releases a job at the same instant in time, and 2. Each task releases subsequent jobs at the earliest instant that it is permitted to do so (i.e., each task releases a new job immediately upon termination of the exclusion window of its previously-released job).

For Liu and Layland, sporadic, multiframe, and GMF task systems, it is well known that a task system τ is preemptive uniprocessor EDF schedulable if and only if EDF meets all deadlines when scheduling its synchronous arrival sequence(s). This has been shown to be equivalent to the following condition:
div.formula: ∀ t>0 τ i ∈τ DBF i (t) ≤ t .
div.p: Techniques essentially identical to those used in demonstrating this can be used to show that the same fact holds for systems of non-cyclic GMF tasks as well (see, e.g., the proof of this fact for systems of GMF tasks in [4]):

During each iteration, DBF i (t) must be computed for each of the tasks τ i ∈ τ . According to Lemma 1, each such computation takes pseudo-polynomial time; since the sum of a polynomial number of pseudo-polynomials is also a pseudo-polynomial, this implies that each iteration takes pseudo-polynomial time. And finally since the product of two pseudo-polynomials is pseudo-polynomial, we may conclude that the total run-time, which is bounded by the product of the number of iterations of the for-loop (a pseudo-polynomial) and the largest run-time for any iteration (also a pseudo-polynomial) is pseudo-polynomial.

div.head: Pragmatic improvements
div.p: Procedure EDF-SCHED(τ ) suffices to demonstrate that EDF schedulability analysis of non-cyclic GMF tasks can be done in pseudo-polynomial time for bounded-utilization task systems. Several optimizations to this procedure are possible; although these optimizations will not reduce the theoretical computational complexity further (i.e., the procedure continues to have pseudo-polynomial worst-case run-time despite them), it is likely that incorporating these optimizations in any implementation significantly improves the run-time behavior observed in practice. We briefly outline some of these optimizations below: §1. In Lemma 2, we focused on demonstrating merely that for non-EDF schedulable bounded-density systems, a pseudo-polynomial upper bound could be obtained on the value of the smallest witness of non-schedulability; we did not attempt to obtain the tightest (i.e., smallest) such bound. With a little effort, bounds that are quite a bit tighter than the one given by Lemma 2 can be obtained. For the case of sporadic tasks, several techniques have been reported in dozens of technical publications, that provide tighter bounds (see, e.g., [16,15,9,17]); we believe that many of these techniques can be adapted for use with the non-cyclic GMF model. Doing so is beneficial, since knowing a smaller upper bound on the witness of the non-schedulability of τ allows us to correspondingly reduce the number of times the for loop of Procedure EDF-SCHED(τ ) must execute. §2. In order to test whether τ i ∈τ DBF i (t) > t for a given value of t, we will compute DBF i (t) for each τ i ∈ τ . The pseudo-polynomial time technique suggested by Lemma 1 (Section 4) for doing this requires that the A i (t ) be determined for all t < t. Of course, an obvious optimization would be to retain these values of the A i (t )'s across iterations of the for-loop, and re-use them when computing the DBF i (t + 1) values. With this optimization, the run-time of each iteration of the for-loop becomes polynomial, rather than pseudo-polynomial. (The overall complexity remains pseudo-polynomial since pseudo-polynomially many iterations of the loop are still needed.) §3. For a given value of t, both Equations 1 and 2 refer back to values of A i (t ); however, no t < (tmax j:0≤j<N I {T i (j)}) appears in these equations. Since we are iterating through the values of t in increasing order, we need only keep the last max j:0≤j<N I {T i (j)} values of A i (t) around, for each τ i ; values of A i (t ) for smaller values of t may safely be discarded. Such an optimization significantly reduces the memory usage, and perhaps avoids the use of secondary storage (and the slow-down that often accompanies the use of external memory). §4. In our pseudo-code representation of Procedure EDF- SCHED(τ ), we had t iterate through every integer value between 1 and the upper bound computed in Lemma 2. In actual fact, however, it can be shown that not all values of t need be tested. We illustrate by a couple of trivial examples:

1. It is immediately obvious that values of t that are smaller than the smallest relative deadline parameter of any task in the system cannot possibly be a witness to the non-schedulability of the system; hence, t may be initialized to min τ i ∈τ (min j:0≤j<N i {D i (j)}) rather than 1.

2. Consider a system τ in which every one of each task's D i (j) and T i (j) parameters is even; it is quite straightforward to observe that if there is a witness to the nonschedulability of this system, then there is an evenvalued witness (and hence it is not necessary to consider odd values of t).

For any given task system, careful analysis of the period and deadline parameters of the tasks typically yields substantial reductions in the number of distinct values of t for which the test of Procedure EDF-SCHED(τ ) must actually be evaluated.

div.head: Context and Conclusions
div.p: As real-time safety-critical application software requirements have become increasingly more complex, there is an increasing need for formal models of real-time processes that satisfy the contradictory properties of (i) being powerful enough to model these complex requirements, and (ii) being efficiently analyzable to ensure that the application systems being designed satisfy basic safety properties. With these twin goals in mind, there has been considerable work done in designing new and powerful models of realtime tasks for which feasibility-analysis remains efficiently do-able. This includes the sporadic tasks model, the multiframe tasks model, the generalized multiframe tasks model and the recurring real-time tasks model [2,3] -this list is by no means exhaustive.

In designing these models, "tractable" has been taken to mean no worse than pseudo-polynomial time for boundedutilization systems (here, "bounded-utilization" means that the asymptotic processor utilization of the task system is bounded from above by a constant strictly less than the computational capacity of the processor). That is, the line demarcating the models considered tractable from the ones considered intractable is whether analysis of boundedutilization systems can be done in pseudo-polynomial time or not: only models for which such pseudo-polynomial analysis is possible are considered tractable. Under this assumption, the recurring real-time tasks model was considered the most general tractable model, in the sense that it generalizes earlier tractable models.

However, the recently-proposed non-cyclic GMF tasks model generalizes the GMF task model in a different direction from the direction that the recurring real-time tasks model does. Our results in this paper establish that EDF schedulability analysis for non-cyclic GMF task systems is also in pseudo-polynomial time for bounded-utilization systems. Hence according to the consensus adopted by the real-time scheduling community, this model, too, is considered tractable. We believe that this fact is of considerable interest, since it allows us to consider models that can be generalized in a different direction from what was previously possible, while retaining tractability. A consequence of this fact is that we can now consider allowing systems designers to build recurrent tasks in which each recurrent task need'nt be characterized by a single period, thereby allowing the system designer a larger space of design possibilities.

Anand et al.[1] do consider a form of non-cyclic behavior for a restricted DAG-based model. However, rather than explicitly dealing with this non-cyclic behavior, the approach adopted in[1] is to approximate it with cyclic behavior by transforming each non-cyclic (called anisochronous in[1]) task to a computationally more demanding cyclic (or isochronous) task.

We note that since EDF is known[10,6] to be an optimal scheduling algorithm on preemptive uniprocessors, EDF schedulability is equivalent to feasibility on such platforms. Thus all our results concerning preemptive uniprocessor EDF-schedulability are equally valid for the preemptive uniprocessor feasibility question: Given a collection τ of non-cyclic GMF tasks, is it the case that for every instance of jobs that can legally be generated by the tasks in τ , there exists a preemptive uniprocessor schedule in which all jobs of all tasks complete by their deadlines?
'Bounded-utilization" means that the asymptotic processor utilization of the task system is bounded from above by a constant strictly less than the computational capacity of the processor.

div.head: Appendix: Hardness of determining DBF
